Question: Can religion be considered a form of science due to its beliefs about life that may not be scientifically proven but are still considered true, such as karma?
Answer: No. And I’m not denigrating religion by saying it, because a lot of things that “aren’t science” are both valid and vital - art, love, ethics, moral responsibility etc. But science isn’t a belief system, except inasmuch as it requires a belief that reality is real, or at least solid enough to be reliably fairly consistent. Science is a *method*, a thing you do. You might as well ask if religion can be considered a form of baking, or fluid mechanics. Science is the process of establishing how physical reality works and what it does by observing it in action, and where possible by thinking of ways to test what you observe and carrying out those tests; then making lists of what you observed and what results you got from any tests which you ran, and analysing the results. Then you think of new ways to tests the results of your analysis, to confirm or disprove them. Religion, like artistic merit, is too nebulous and subjective for that kind of testing.

Question: Does every species go extinct at some point in its existence?
Answer: It’s a matter of definition. Every species will *eventually* become extinct, because eventually the universe itself will decay to the point where it can no longer support life. Before that, every species will eventually cease to exist as a species, but whether it becomes extinct or not is, again, a matter of definition. Many merely become “pseudo-extinct”, which means that the species has living descendants, but over time those descendants become different enough that were they to meet their ancestors, they could not interbreed. Every species alive today is descended from many thousands of earlier species which became pseudo-extinct rather than fully extinct, as by definition they have living descendants. [Note that this doesn’t mean you can derive a figure for extinct species by multiplying living ones by ten thousand, because pedigree collapse also exists at this level, meaning that there are usually multiple modern descendants from the *same* line of ancestors.]

Question: If there were a society that did not use a monetary system, but rather just working and doing your part for society was enough to warrant getting everything you want for free, would you live there?
Answer: The problem is that it’s very difficult to make it work on the large scale with our present rate of technology, because we need ways of apportioning scarce resources and labour to where they’re needed without exploiting particular groups. The best way to do that is that if we need people to do things they would rather not do or give us things they would rather keep, we give them something in exchange that they like better or need more, and money is a way of keeping score of favours exchanged. We can manage without money in small groups such as kibbutzim or Amazon tribes, where exchanges are small and local and it’s easy to keep track of “If you help me to sheer my sheep today I’ll let you borrow my boat next week”. We could also do it in a Star Trek-style post-scarcity society, where resources could be obtained with little effort or labour, and the tedious or dangerous jobs that humans would rather not do could all be done by machines, leaving people to do jobs they didn’t need to be incentivised to do, because they just enjoyed them. And yes, I’d enjoy living there. There would still be plenty of work that people could do if they wanted to work: artistic creation, handcrafting, research etc. We see already that people are keen to get handmade rather than mass-produced goods, and prefer to be helped by people rather than machines, and even if you didn’t need to earn money from what you made people would still do it for the status and appreciation. Winning the annual award for best architectural design or greatest contribution to research or most helpful customer service would still be worth it for the honour, even if we didn’t need a monetary prize to pay our rent. You can see a microcosm of it in the fanfiction world. By definition people don’t make any money from fanfiction or fanart, other than what may be needed to cover their costs (especially before the internet, when fanzines had to be printed), but people work hard at it because they enjoy doing it, they enjoy the praise for a job well done, and keeping the fanfiction scene going gives them access to other people’s work that they enjoy reading.

Question: How does the existence of the Platypus fit into the theory of evolution?
Answer: Monotremes are a side branch that split off the mammals early on, so even though they have come as far from that split as any other mammal, they have retained some pre-mammalian characteristics, such as laying eggs and having a cloaca. They are also borderline on that whole “mammal” thing, because their milk production isn’t very sophisticated. They don’t have nipples - they split away before those evolved - and the mother just oozes milk out onto her belly where the young lap it up. A side effect of this is that since the young don’t suckle as such, they don’t need purseable lips. This has freed them to develop hard and specialised mouths, like a rubbery version of a bird’s beak but lined with sensors. Echidnas use theirs for probing termite mounds, and platypuses use theirs for rummaging in underwater mud in the dark, looking for small prey.

Question: After an explosion, things are destroyed, but after the Big Bang, the universe and everything in it were created. So, is there no powerful intelligent brain behind it? Was it possible without any interference or intervention?

There was no ordered thing - there was no *thing* - before the Big Bang (and no time, so “before” isn’t really meaningful), and it was a rapid expansion rather than an explosion. Kind of like blowing air into a balloon, but with extra dimensions. The problem is one of language. “Explosion” has a literal meaning, but it also has a metaphorical meaning which is often quite different from the literal one. The so-called “Cambrian Explosion”, for example, was a biological arms race which took at least 20 million years, and resembled an actual explosion only in that something - in this case, the roster of phyla - got bigger about three times faster than usual.

Question: Why are there more human-like fossils than ape-like fossils, even though we share a common ancestor with chimpanzees and gorillas (excluding hominids)?

Because the other great apes tend to live in dense jungle, and it’s not an environment that favours fossilisation. It’s hot and damp so bodies decay quickly, and the soil is full of roots so it’s rare for bodies to end up buried. Humans lived out on the plains where bodies were more likely to mummify and harden and then be buried by drifting soil, and more recently we took to actually burying our dead.

Question: Could there be other large carnivorous theropod dinosaurs that were potentially bigger than Tyrannosaurus rex, but we are unaware due to limited evidence?

The fact that all the really huge theropods we know about had tiny arms suggests to me that they had reached their size limit. The only reason I can see for losing their arms is that if they had large arms they would need either smaller heads (and therefore jaws) or a longer, heavier tail, to remain balanced at the hip, and if they got any heavier they would no longer be able to run. So they probably didn’t and couldn’t get a lot bigger than T-rex.

Question: How long did it take for humans to evolve from apes? Why did apes not also evolve into humans?
Answer: Apes did evolve into humans. Humans are a type of great ape. It took us four or five million years to get from the point where our line split from the line that led to chimps, to the dawn of genus Homo, and another two million years to get to Homo sapiens. The reason only one line of apes became human is that only one line of apes moved out onto the open plains, where conditions favoured increasing bipedalism. Full bipedalism enabled us to develop more dexterous hands which didn’t need to double as walking feet, and having more dexterous hands made it an advantage to develop bigger brains for designing better, more complex tools which we now had the ability to build and handle. Bigger brains were a double-edged sword, because they take a lot of energy to run and they make childbirth more difficult, requiring wider hips which make running fast more difficult. So we didn’t develop them until we had the dexterous hands for handling the complex tools, which made the advantages of big brains outweigh the disadvantages.

Question: Can you still love an author's work even if in real life that author is transphobic?

Steinbeck was said to be a horrible person in real life, but we admire his writing. We still admire the beautiful sculptures of Eric Gill, and nobody is calling for their removal, even though he was an all-purpose pervert who had sex not only with his children but with his dog. We still revere Charlie Chaplin, even though he was a bit of a hebephile even by the standards of the 1930s. We even admire the films of Leni Riefenstahl even though some of them were produced for the Nazis. We can still appreciate the artistry while rejecting the message. But the band LostProphets went into free-fall when it was revealed that their lead singer’s hobby was raping infants, and I don’t think I could separate the crime from the performance. Part of it is that with a singer you have to interact with the actual performer, whereas a book or a sculpture is at a remove from the person who created them. Question: If all animals except for one species were to go extinct, which species would you choose to be the dominant one in the new world?

Assuming that we’re ruling out humans, how about leaf sheep? Once they’ve taken in enough algae to populate their fronds, they barely need to eat at all, just live off the sugars the algae produce. And we know that in the past something very similar to a modern sea-slug branched off and gave rise to the cephalopods, and that molluscs can live both on land and in the sea, so the descendants of this sea slug would have a decent chance of spreading out and repopulating the world. On the other hand, if you want a vertebrate I’d probably go for raccoons. They could live entirely on plants if they needed to, they’re intelligent and they have good hands, so they could develop a new sapient species fairly easily, and they don’t breed so fast that in the absence of predators they would overpopulate and then starve, as rats would. Or orangutans, ditto: they’re the most nearly herbivorous great ape.

Question: Why do koalas not recognize eucalyptus leaves as food unless it’s on a tree branch?

They’re quite happy to eat leaves which have been picked but which are still effectively “on the vine”, because that way they retain their moisture, but leaves which have been picked off their stems are effectively toxic to them. It would also be mechanically difficult for them to pick the leaves up without a stem to hold them by - but they will eat apples, because there’s enough there to get a grip on.

Question: Does Great Britain have a constitutional guarantee of free expression similar to America's First Amendment right to "freedom of speech"?

So there are laws governing a few forms of speech - libel, betraying state secrets, certain kinds of reporting on court cases while they are in progress, certain kinds of obscenity (ie circulating paedophile material), false advertising, and hate speech of a kind likely to incite violence. Other than that, anything goes.

Question: Do all birds lay eggs? If not, which ones don't lay eggs and how did this trait evolve in those species (if it did)?
Answer: All modern birds lay eggs, and as far as we know so did all extinct birds. Laying eggs means they don’t have to carry the weight of a pregnancy as they fly, and even for flightless birds, laying eggs doesn’t have any strong disadvantages which might lead them to evolve to be ovo-viviparous (retaining the egg inside the body and then giving live birth) instead. It is quite possible, however, that in the far future a penguin or auk might evolve to be ovoviviparous, just as the ichthyosaurs did. It would enable them to become wholly aquatic and give birth in the water, instead of having to come ashore to nest. Or the ones that live in the tropics might evolve to do the turtle thing: crawl up the beach for an hour a year, lay their eggs in the hot sand and then abandon them.

Question: Why did evolution not lead to humans living for thousands of years in their fertile, 35-year-old bodies to maximize reproduction?
Answer: Because until about 80 years ago, with the discovery of penicillin, the odds were good that we would still die of disease or accident before we were 70. There’s no evolutionary advantage in having the *potential* to stop aging and live for thousands of years if you’re still going to die of a dental abscess at 45, so natural selection pushed us to get our breeding done early. Also, maximising reproduction isn’t a good thing if you are near the top of the food chain, because then you use up all your resources and starve. Fast breeding is for species that are low in the food chain, and have to struggle to survive predation. A female rat can quite easily produce 80 babies during her life, but on average only two will survive to breeding age in turn.

Question: Why didn't birds evolve to the huge sizes of pterodalctyls when they became extinct 66 mya? Is it possible for a giraffe-sized flying bird to exist (since the largest of pterodactyls were giraffe-sized)?
Answer: No. Birds have a fundamental problem which limits their size. They take off by leaping up using their legs, but once they are airborne then their leg muscles are no longer contributing to flight and become dead weight they have to carry. And they can’t jettison them as a rocket jettisons spent fuel tanks: they’re stuck with carrying them. Evidently the weight of their legs increases faster than their strength does, so they hit a point where in order to carry their legs they need wings so big and heavy that they need stronger, heavier legs in order to take off, which then need bigger, heavier wings to carry them…. But pterosaurs had hands at the middle of the wing, and flung themselves into the air by slamming their hands to the ground and pushing up with their wing muscles. They used the *same* muscles to take off and to fly, so the extra muscle needed to propel a very large pterosaur into the air didn’t become dead weight once they were airborne, but then contributed to keeping them up.

Question: What are epigenetic make it short?
Answer: The DNA in your chromosomes is supported on a spine of proteins called histones. The shape of the histone spine affects how accessible a given stretch of DNA - a gene - is and therefore how likely that gene is to be activated. Some living conditions, such as a prolonged famine, can affect the shape of the histone spine, making particular genes more or less accessible and therefore more or less likely to be activated. Because of prolonged natural selection, these changes generally happen in ways which activate genes which help us to cope with the conditions which caused the change. E.g. they might make us better at storing fat in order to cope with a famine. We call these changes epigenetic tags. They can be passed on for at least a couple of generations, so the children of people who survived a famine will still have their chromosomes tweaked to make them better at coping with famine.

Question: Attention evolutionists, your theory is now proven false. We have been aging and dying for thousands of years, yet we have not evolved to counter aging at all. Does this not show evolution is false since this is a prime situation for it to occur?
Answer: This is probably a troll question, since it uses the fake word "evolutionist", but it's still a question many people fail to understand. Evolution works via differences in reproductive success. Family lines which are good at having a lot of surviving offspring get to spread their genes. Humans *have already* evolved to have an unusually long lifespan for a creature our size, exactly because grandparents help with raising the young, and therefore continue to have an effect on the reproductive success of their family line until their grandchildren are in their early teens. As to why animals do not generally live to very great age, you have to consider that in a state of nature (and that includes humans until fairly recently, in evolutionary terms), individuals rarely get to die of old age. They get eaten, or they have an accident, or they die of disease, long before age takes them. Even in humans, the average age at death is decades lower than the maximum age, as so many of us succumb to cancer or heart disease. There is no benefit to an animal in having the *capacity* to live for centuries if it's going to be killed and eaten when it's seven. It needs to get its breeding done early, before something kills it, so selection pressure tends to favour having offspring early in life, and the selection pressure to prolong life gets weaker and weaker once you've already passed on your genes and you get past the point at which the likelihood is that you're about to be killed by something anyway. Only animals which are virtually predator-proof and/or live in very safe environments can afford to live long, leisurely lives and reproduce slowly, as we see in Greenland sharks, baleen whales and elephants. We can see this demonstrated most strikingly by the naked mole rat. They're the size of a hamster, and animals that size normally live one to seven years. But because the naked mole rat spends most of its life tunnelling underground and dragigng plants down into its tunnels by the roots, they are at very little risk from any cause of death and so live thirty or more years: extraordinarily long for a smallish rodent.

Question: Is it true that being a woman is not based on what you wear or how you style your hair, but the chromosomes you possess?
Answer: No. Chromosomes have little to do with it. At its most basic, the sex of a therian mammal embryo is determined by a gene called SRY, which is usually but not always situated on a Y chromosome. Absence or failure of the SRY gene results in a female-form embryo, although they may or may not be fertile. Some XY women are fertile and able to get pregnant, but XX men are always sterile (and I’m not talking about trans people here but fully cisgender individuals). Then, even if the person has no Y-chromosome and no SRY gene, under some circumstances they may not develop as a normal female, especially if they either have only one X-chromosome, and /or are exposed to androgens during development. They may have no gonads, or combined ovotestes, or masculinised genitalia, with a penis combined with a womb and ovaries. They may have a masculinised body-map, resulting in a person whose body is female but whose brain is trying to map to a male body (F2M trans). Then, even if the SRY gene is normally situated on a Y chromosome it may fail to work properly, or the body may fail to respond normally to it, or their hormones may not match. From this, we get people with an entirely female and very feminine body-plan and appearance, but no womb, and undescended testicles instead of ovaries; and people with a feminised body-map, resulting in a person whose body is male but whose brain is trying to map to a female body (M2F trans). People who are XXY or XXXY will be mostly male (assuming there’s an SRY gene present on the Y chromosome), but quite feminised. Finally, male and female twin embryos may fuse in the womb, resulting in an individual who is a mix of XX and XY cells and of male and female parts.

Question: Why do we say that most modern humans descended from just two individuals? How is this possible if our ancestors were numerous throughout history and even now?

As you go further back in time you get “pedigree collapse”, meaning that you and your neighbours start sharing ancestors. Trace your male line ancestors back and eventually you’ll hit a point where your male line ancestor is also the male line ancestor of a guy from the next village. Y-chromosome Adam is the most recent man who is *everybody*’s male line ancestor, and mitochondrial Eve is the most recent woman who is everybody’s female line ancestor. But they didn’t live in the same time and place, and there were thousands, maybe tens of thousands of other men and women who were alive in their day and from whom you are descended: but those others are e.g. your mother’s father’s mother’s father’s father’s mother’s mother’s father’s mother, not your direct male line or female line ancestor.

Question: Why are certain animals born with the ability to walk, but not humans?
Answer: Having “altricial” babies who are born at an early stage of development is usually done so that the mother can carry a large litter and have more babies at a time. Having precocial babies (born able to get up and run) usually means the mother will only have room for one or two. Humans and bears are unusual in that we have only one or two babies, but they’re altricial. In bears it’s so they can give birth during hibernation and the babies can stay small and not needing much milk until the mother is ready to wake up fully and start hunting again. In humans, it’s the price we pay for high intelligence. Mammal brain tissue is inefficiently bulky, meaning that high intelligence requires a large head. A large head requires a wide pelvis in order to be born. If our babies were born at a later stage, the mother’s pelvis would need to be so wide she could barely walk. Of course, that doesn’t explain why our babies aren’t born tiny but walking, but as far as I know no mammal does this. Precocial babies are always fairly big relative to the mother. There must be some practical or developmental reason for this, but I don’t know what it is.
